newsitem.title: UK: Stg stages quick recovery from post-Waigel lows.
newsitem.headline: Stg stages quick recovery from post-Waigel lows.

text.p: Sterling bobbed back up towards six-and-a-half-year highs against the mark, only briefly fazed after German finance minister Theo Waigel suggested its recent surge against the mark was unjustified by economic fundamentals.
Traders drove the pound down nearly two pfennigs to 3.0045 marks after Waigel said the dollar and the pound's strength against the mark was an overreaction by the market.

He added Germany was interested in a strong mark and that it was in contact with other members of the Group of Seven leading industrial nations, raising the spectre of concerted central bank intervention.
The pound staged a full recovery in little more than an hour, though, as traders bet intervention was not imminent.
"The German comments triggered some strength in the mark but then the pound bounced strongly back in our faces," said Dave Eddy, the chief trader at Sumitomo Bank.
Sterling/mark was at 3.0260/70 at 0955 GMT from 3.0200/10 late Monday in Europe. Its rebound took it to within a quarter-pfennig of Monday's 80-month peak of 3.0327 at one point.
Cable was at $1.6858/68 from $1.6880/90 Monday. The pound's trade-weighted index was at 105.6, compared with the near-seven-year high of 105.7 it reached on Monday.
Traders also expect expectations of higher UK interest rates and a broad-based European economic and monetary union to continue to buoy the pound in the coming months.

"A lot of people are still pessimistic about the mark's prospects against the pound and the dollar," said Eric Fishwick, analyst at Nikko Europe. "They still see safe have arguments which will encourage flows into safe havens into anything which is going to be outside EMU."
Speculation that the planned European single currency will not be as strong as the mark have spurred traders to move into currencies which are not involved in the project.

The UK, which is expected to exercise its EMU opt-out, is also attracting traders because of expectations that UK interest rates are set to rise further, increasing the premium they offer over rates in continental Europe.

At 6.75 percent, UK base rates are already 3.5 percentage points above Germany's securities repurchase rate. Moreover, the September short sterling contract is now at 92.84, implying rates of 7.16 percent by the end of the third quarter.
"The Bank of England is faced with a loose fiscal policy and feels that monetary policy should be tightened," said Fishwick at Nikko, who expects sterling to benefit from this policy mix.
Sterling's 25 percent surge since August 1996 in trade-weighted terms is denting UK exporters' competitiveness.

Only yesterday, the chairman of Thorn Plc told shareholders that sterling strength would reduce current year profits by 11 million pounds, around eight percent of this year's expected pre-tax profits.
Still, traders are not yet overly concerned that the Bank of England will mount a determined effort to halt its rally.
"The markets are generally a lot more relaxed about the threat of forex intervention," said Nikko's Fishwick. "European central banks seem unwilling to intervene against market flows."
